title: Elephants in the Alps: The Podcast Rewriting History If Carthage Had Crushed Rome
summary: What if Hannibal's elephants had actually finished the job? A new episode of the podcast 'Almost History' dives into that tantalizing alternate reality, examining how the ancient Mediterranean—and by extension, our modern world—might look if Carthage had defeated the Roman Republic. The Punic Wars, fought between 264 and 146 B.C., were a clash of superpowers. Rome ultimately won, building an empire that shaped Western civilization. But it was a near thing. During the Second Punic War, the Carthaginian general Hannibal led an army—including war elephants—across the Alps and inflicted devastating defeats on Roman legions. At one point, Rome was on the brink of collapse. Historian and archaeologist Eve MacDonald, author of 'Carthage: A New History of an Ancient Empire,' tells host Emily Staniforth that Carthage had 'enormous resources' and the fight was far from one-sided. Yet she also notes a grim reality: 'I always think the Romans were probably never going to go away.' Their resilience and manpower were almost inexhaustible. Still, the podcast explores the turning points where a few different decisions could have tipped the balance. A Carthaginian victory would have meant a Mediterranean dominated by a North African commercial empire rather than a European military one. Trade routes, cultural exchange, and the distribution of power would have shifted southward. MacDonald emphasizes that we've lost the stories of Carthage, Phoenicia, and Numidia, so our understanding of the ancient world is lopsided. 'As much as the Greco-Roman history of the Mediterranean is part of the Western world, so too is all of Carthage,' she says. The episode is part of a series that tackles historical pivot points, from D-Day failing to the Bolshevik Revolution never happening. It's a reminder that history is not a straight line but a web of possibilities. You can listen on Acast and imagine a world where Roman ruins are a footnote and Carthaginian ports dominate the coastline. What language would you be speaking? What stories would you know? The podcast doesn't just answer questions—it plants new ones.
why_it_matters: By playing out plausible alternate histories, the podcast reveals that the world we live in was shaped by fragile moments, encouraging us to question which stories get remembered and whose voices are lost—a skill that matters when studying history and current events.

background_read: The Punic Wars (264–146 B.C.) were a clash between two superpowers of the ancient Mediterranean: Rome, then a rising republic, and Carthage, a wealthy North African city-state founded by Phoenician traders.
Hannibal (the Carthaginian general) famously marched war elephants through the Alps in 218 B.C. and crushed several Roman armies; for a moment, Rome was on the verge of total collapse.

Carthage’s culture and records were largely destroyed when Rome finally burned the city, meaning most of what we know comes from Greek and Roman writers—a classic case of history written by the winners.
Eve MacDonald (a historian and author of 'Carthage: A New History of an Ancient Empire') is one of the researchers working to recover the lost voices of Carthage, Phoenicia, and Numidia.
The podcast 'Almost History' uses a counterfactual approach—asking 'what if?'—to highlight how fragile pivotal moments really were, from ancient wars to 20th‑century revolutions.

HISTORICAL CONTEXT: The Punic Wars (264–146 B.C.) were a superpower struggle; Rome ultimately won but came terrifyingly close to losing.
└─ DETAIL: During the Second Punic War, Hannibal crossed the Alps, inflicted devastating defeats, and brought Rome to the brink of collapse.

└─ QUOTE: 'I always think the Romans were probably never going to go away.' But small changes could have tipped the balance.
IMPLICATIONS: A Carthaginian victory would have created a Mediterranean dominated by a North African commercial empire instead of a European military one.
└─ LOST NARRATIVES: MacDonald points out we’ve lost the stories of Carthage, Phoenicia, and Numidia, making our view of the ancient world lopsided.

perspectives.description: Bringing counterfactual history to a wide audience makes the ancient world feel alive and relevant. Listeners who might never read a textbook can get hooked on big ideas, sparking genuine curiosity about archaeology and classics.

Some historians worry that 'what if' games oversimplify complex events. They risk reducing real suffering to a fun thought experiment and distracting from the actual causes of Rome’s victory—like its deep manpower reserves and political adaptability.

The exercise highlights how history is always told from a viewpoint: because Carthage was destroyed, its stories were erased. By reconstructing lost perspectives, we see that our understanding of the past is always incomplete and shaped by power.

If popular media continues to explore alternate histories, it could encourage new generations to pursue research into under‑studied civilizations like Carthage, potentially leading to fresh archaeological discoveries and more balanced global narratives.
